position: both — mostly before a noun: *an a cappella group*; after a verb: *the whole album is a cappella*
form: from Italian *a cappella*, 'in the style of the chapel'
contrast: In *They sang a cappella* the phrase is an adverb, the most common use; the adjective is the one before a noun or after *be*.

senses.gloss: Sung by voices alone, without musical instruments.
examples: She joined an *a cappella* group in college.
The last song on the album is *a cappella*.
They gave an *a cappella* performance of the national anthem.

type: classifying — how things are priced and sold
position: both — *an a la carte menu*; *everything here is a la carte*
form: from French *à la carte*, 'by the menu'; Americans usually write it without the accent
contrast: In *You can order a la carte* the phrase is an adverb. Outside restaurants it means 'chosen one by one': *a la carte cable channels*.

senses.gloss: Chosen and paid for item by item, not as part of a set meal or package.
examples: The *a la carte* menu is more expensive than the lunch special.
At this steakhouse the side dishes are *a la carte*.
More people want *a la carte* streaming plans instead of big bundles.

position: after the noun — *pie a la mode*, never *a la mode pie*
form: from French *à la mode*, 'in the fashion'
contrast: A trap for anyone who knows French: in American English it almost always means 'served with ice cream', not 'fashionable'.

senses.gloss: Served with a scoop of ice cream on top or on the side.
examples: I'll have the apple pie *a la mode*, please.
The diner is famous for its peach cobbler *a la mode*.
Do you want your brownie *a la mode*?

position: both — mostly before a noun: *a priori knowledge*; after a verb: *the claim is a priori*

senses.gloss: Based on reasoning or assumptions rather than on observation or experience.
examples: Philosophers argue about whether math is *a priori* knowledge.
There's no *a priori* reason to think the new drug won't work.
His argument rests on a few *a priori* assumptions about human nature.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *everything is A-OK*; before a noun: *an A-OK job*
form: *A* + *OK*, first used in the US space program

senses.gloss: Completely fine; in perfect order.
examples: The doctor said I'm *A-OK* to go back to work.
Don't worry, the car is *A-OK* now.
She gave us the *A-OK* sign from the stage.

position: both — *an abandoned house*; *the factory has been abandoned for years*

senses.gloss: Left empty and no longer used or looked after.
examples: Kids used to play in the *abandoned* warehouse by the river.
Police found an *abandoned* car on the side of the highway.
The old mining town looks completely *abandoned*.

senses.gloss: Left alone by the people who should take care of it.
examples: The shelter takes in *abandoned* dogs and cats.
He felt *abandoned* when his father moved away.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *she looked abashed*; also *an abashed smile*
contrast: The opposite *unabashed* (*an unabashed fan*) is more common today than *abashed* itself.

senses.gloss: Embarrassed or ashamed, especially after being caught or corrected.
examples: He looked a little *abashed* when the teacher read his note out loud.
She was not the least bit *abashed* by the criticism.
The boys stood there, *abashed*, while their mother cleaned up the mess.

position: both — *an abbreviated version*; *the name is often abbreviated*

senses.gloss: Made shorter than the full form or the usual length.
examples: "Dept." is the *abbreviated* form of "department."
Because of the storm, the game was played in an *abbreviated* season.
We only had time for an *abbreviated* meeting.

position: attributive only — *abdominal pain*; after a verb say *in the abdomen*
contrast: The plural noun *abdominals* (or *abs*) means the stomach muscles: *work on your abs*.

senses.gloss: In or relating to the stomach area of the body.
examples: He went to the ER with severe *abdominal* pain.
These exercises strengthen your *abdominal* muscles.
The doctor ordered an *abdominal* ultrasound.

position: both — *aberrant behavior*; *the result was aberrant*

senses.gloss: Different from what is normal or expected, usually in a bad way.
examples: Scientists threw out one *aberrant* result from the study.
His *aberrant* behavior worried his teachers.
One cold week in July is not that *aberrant* for this city.

position: both — *an abhorrent practice*; *the idea is abhorrent to me*

senses.gloss: Morally unacceptable and causing strong disgust.
examples: Racism is *abhorrent* to everyone in this room.
The report described *abhorrent* conditions at the prison.
Of all his crimes, lying to the families was the most *abhorrent*.

position: attributive only — *an abiding love*; after a verb say *lasting*
contrast: *Law-abiding* (*a law-abiding citizen*) comes from *abide by* 'obey' and has a different meaning.

senses.gloss: Lasting for a long time and not changing.
examples: She has an *abiding* love of the ocean.
His *abiding* interest in history started with his grandfather's stories.
Our *abiding* memory of that trip is the kindness of strangers.

position: attributive only — *abject poverty*, *an abject apology*

senses.gloss: Extremely bad and without hope, used about poverty, misery or failure.
examples: Millions of people still live in *abject* poverty.
The launch was an *abject* failure.

senses.gloss: Showing no pride or self-respect.
examples: He made an *abject* apology to the whole team.
She looked at him with *abject* fear.

position: both — *able-bodied adults*; *anyone who is able-bodied can help*

senses.gloss: Physically strong and healthy, without a disability.
examples: The program requires *able-bodied* adults to work or look for work.
We need every *able-bodied* volunteer to fill sandbags.
Some of the buildings were designed only for people who are *able-bodied*.

position: both — *abnormal results*; *his heart rate was abnormal*
contrast: *Abnormal* is formal and often medical. For a strange person in everyday speech Americans say *weird* or *strange*; calling someone *abnormal* sounds insulting.

senses.gloss: Different from what is usual or expected, often in a way that suggests a problem.
examples: The blood test showed some *abnormal* results.
It's not *abnormal* for toddlers to throw tantrums.
This has been the *most abnormal* winter anyone can remember.

position: both — *abominable weather*; *the service was abominable*

senses.gloss: Extremely bad, unpleasant or wrong.
examples: The way they treated those workers was *abominable*.
We had *abominable* weather the whole week.
It was the *most abominable* meal I've ever paid for.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *aboriginal peoples*
contrast: For Australia it is capitalized: *Aboriginal art*. About Native Americans, Americans say *Native American* or *Indigenous*, not *aboriginal*.

senses.gloss: Living or existing in a place from the earliest times, before anyone arrived from elsewhere.
examples: Canada recognizes the rights of its *aboriginal* peoples.
The island still has patches of *aboriginal* forest.

senses.gloss: Relating to the first peoples of Australia; written with a capital A.
examples: The museum has a large collection of *Aboriginal* art.
She studies *Aboriginal* languages of northern Australia.

position: attributive only — *an abortive attempt*; after a verb say *failed* or *unsuccessful*
contrast: Despite the look of the word, it has nothing to do with medical abortion in everyday use; it means a plan or attempt that failed.

senses.gloss: Failing before it could be completed.
examples: After an *abortive* attempt to fix the sink, he called a plumber.
The general was jailed after an *abortive* coup.
Their *abortive* peace talks ended after two days.

position: attributive only — *the above-mentioned document*
contrast: Formal, used in letters, contracts and reports. *The above-mentioned* can also stand alone as a noun: *the above-mentioned will attend*.

senses.gloss: Mentioned earlier in the same document or text.
examples: Please send the *above-mentioned* forms by Friday.
The *above-mentioned* tenant has not paid rent since March.
None of the *above-mentioned* problems have been fixed.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *the deal was aboveboard*; also *an aboveboard deal*
form: compound — *above* + *board*, from card players keeping their hands above the table

senses.gloss: Honest and legal, with nothing hidden.
examples: I checked, and the whole sale was completely *aboveboard*.
He promised the investors that everything was *aboveboard*.
We want an *aboveboard* process that the public can trust.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *an aboveground pool*; after a verb: *the pipes are aboveground*

senses.gloss: Built or located above the surface of the ground.
examples: We bought an *aboveground* pool for the backyard.
The city is replacing *aboveground* power lines with buried cables.
Most of the tank is *aboveground*, so it's easy to inspect.

position: both — *an abrasive cleaner*; *her manner can be abrasive*

senses.gloss: Rough enough to scratch or rub a surface clean.
examples: Don't use an *abrasive* sponge on nonstick pans.
Sandpaper is *abrasive* by design.

senses.gloss: Rude and harsh in a way that annoys people.
examples: The new manager's *abrasive* style upset the whole office.
He's smart, but he can be *more abrasive* than he realizes.

position: both — *an abridged edition*; *this version is abridged*

senses.gloss: Made shorter by removing parts, used about books, speeches and recordings.
examples: I listened to the *abridged* audiobook on the drive.
The school uses an *abridged* edition of the novel.
Be careful: the copy on the website is *abridged*.

position: both — *an abrupt stop*; *his answer was abrupt*

senses.gloss: Sudden and unexpected.
examples: The bus came to an *abrupt* stop.
Her career came to an *abrupt* end after the scandal.
The change in weather was *more abrupt* than forecasters expected.

senses.gloss: Speaking or acting in a short way that seems rude or unfriendly.
examples: Sorry if I was *abrupt* on the phone; I was in a hurry.
He gave an *abrupt* answer and walked away.

position: both — the 'complete' sense only before a noun: *an absolute mess*; the others also after a verb: *his power was absolute*
contrast: The adverb *absolutely* is far more common in speech: *Absolutely!* means 'yes, definitely'.

senses.gloss: Complete and total, used to make a noun stronger.
examples: The house was an *absolute* mess after the party.
That's *absolute* nonsense, and you know it.
We waited in *absolute* silence.

senses.gloss: Not limited or controlled in any way.
examples: The king had *absolute* power over his people.
Freedom of speech is important, but it is not *absolute*.

senses.gloss: Measured on its own, not in comparison with something else.
examples: In *absolute* terms, the company earned more this year.
The *absolute* value of -5 is 5.

position: both — *an absolutist regime*; *her views on free speech are absolutist*
contrast: Also a noun: *He's a free-speech absolutist*.

senses.gloss: Believing that a ruler or government should have unlimited power.
examples: The country was under *absolutist* rule for two centuries.
Historians compare the two *absolutist* monarchies.

senses.gloss: Holding a principle so firmly that no exceptions are allowed.
examples: She takes an *absolutist* position on privacy.
His views became *more absolutist* as he got older.

position: both — *absorbent paper towels*; *this fabric is very absorbent*
contrast: *Absorbent* soaks up liquid; *absorbing* means very interesting.

senses.gloss: Able to soak up liquid easily.
examples: Use an *absorbent* cloth to clean up the spill.
Cotton towels are *more absorbent* than polyester ones.
The soil here is sandy and very *absorbent*.

position: both — *an absorbing book*; *the documentary was absorbing*
form: -ing — what holds your attention; *absorbed* is the person who feels it
contrast: *The book was absorbing*, but *I was absorbed in the book*. *Absorbent* is about soaking up liquid.

senses.gloss: So interesting that it holds all your attention.
examples: It's an *absorbing* story about a family in 1930s Texas.
I found the lecture surprisingly *absorbing*.
Of all her novels, this is the *most absorbing*.

position: both — *an abstract idea*; *the question is too abstract*
contrast: Many Americans also stress the adjective ab-STRAKT; the verb *abstract* is always ab-STRAKT. The noun *abstract* is a summary of a scientific paper.

senses.gloss: Based on ideas rather than on real, physical things or specific examples.
examples: Justice and freedom are *abstract* concepts.
Can you give me an example? This is all a bit *abstract*.
Algebra felt *more abstract* to me than geometry.

senses.gloss: In art, using shapes and colors instead of showing people or objects as they look.
examples: The museum's second floor is all *abstract* art.
Her later paintings became completely *abstract*.

position: both — *an abstruse theory*; *the article was abstruse*

senses.gloss: Difficult to understand because it is complicated or specialized.
examples: The professor lost the class in an *abstruse* discussion of tax law.
Most people find these legal arguments pretty *abstruse*.
It's one of the *most abstruse* books I've ever tried to read.

position: both — *an absurd idea*; *that's absurd*
takes: *to*-infinitive after *it*: *It's absurd to charge that much*; *that*-clause

senses.gloss: Completely unreasonable or silly.
examples: Twenty dollars for a hot dog? That's *absurd*.
It's *absurd* to think one person could do all this work.
The plot gets *more absurd* with every episode.

position: both — *abundant rainfall*; *fish are abundant in the lake*
takes: *in* + noun — having a lot of something: *a region abundant in oil*

senses.gloss: Existing in large amounts; more than enough.
examples: The area has *abundant* natural resources.
Deer are *abundant* in these woods.
Hydrogen is the *most abundant* element in the universe.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *abused children*; after a verb: *the dog had been abused*
contrast: The adjective is pronounced with /z/ (uh-BYOOZD), like the verb; the noun *abuse* ends in /s/.

senses.gloss: Treated cruelly or violently, especially over a long time.
examples: The center offers shelter to *abused* women and their kids.
They adopted an *abused* horse from a rescue farm.
Many of the children in the program were *abused* at home.

position: both — *an abusive husband*; *the coach was verbally abusive*

senses.gloss: Treating someone with cruelty or violence.
examples: She finally left an *abusive* relationship.
He grew up with an *abusive* father.

senses.gloss: Using rude and insulting words.
examples: The fan was thrown out for shouting *abusive* language at the players.
Customers who get *abusive* with staff will be asked to leave.

senses.gloss: Using power or a system wrongly or unfairly.
examples: The lawsuit accuses the lender of *abusive* practices.
New rules target the *most abusive* debt collectors.

position: predicative only — *the town was abuzz*; never before a noun

senses.gloss: Full of excited talk or activity.
examples: The office was *abuzz* with news of the merger.
Social media is *abuzz* about the new trailer.
By noon the whole school was *abuzz*.

position: both — *abysmal service*; *the ratings were abysmal*

senses.gloss: Extremely bad.
senses.ru: ужасный, отвратительный, из рук вон плохой
examples: The team's defense was *abysmal* last night.
Customer service at that store is *abysmal*.
It was the *most abysmal* quarter in the company's history.

position: both — the school sense mostly before a noun: *the academic year*; the others also after a verb: *the point is academic*
contrast: Russian *академический отпуск* is *a leave of absence*, not an academic vacation. The noun *an academic* means a university teacher or researcher.

senses.gloss: Relating to schools, colleges and studying.
examples: The *academic* year starts in late August.
She got an *academic* scholarship to Stanford.
His *academic* record is excellent.

senses.gloss: Good at studying from books, rather than practical or technical work.
examples: My brother was never very *academic*, but he's a great mechanic.
The program is *more academic* than most trade schools.

senses.gloss: Of theoretical interest only, because it makes no practical difference.
senses.ru: чисто теоретический, не имеющий практического значения
examples: Whether we could have won is *academic* now.
The debate is purely *academic* since the store already closed.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *an accelerated program*

senses.gloss: Happening or done faster than usual.
examples: She finished an *accelerated* nursing program in eighteen months.
The tree showed *accelerated* growth after the rain.
Smart kids are sometimes put in *accelerated* math classes.

position: both — *accented English*; *the second syllable is accented*

senses.gloss: Spoken with an accent from another country or region.
examples: He speaks fluent but heavily *accented* English.
Her voice was soft and slightly *accented*.

senses.gloss: Said with more force or stress than the syllables around it.
examples: In "banana," the middle syllable is *accented*.
Mark the *accented* syllable in each word.

position: both — *acceptable behavior*; *the price is acceptable*
takes: *to* + person: *acceptable to both sides*; *to*-infinitive after *it*: *It's not acceptable to yell at staff*

senses.gloss: Good enough, or allowed because most people agree it is fine.
examples: Is it *acceptable* to wear jeans to the office?
We need a solution that is *acceptable* to everyone.
Working from home is *more acceptable* now than it was ten years ago.

position: both — *accepted practice*; *the theory is widely accepted*

senses.gloss: Generally agreed to be true, correct or normal.
examples: It's an *accepted* fact that smoking causes cancer.
Tipping twenty percent is the *accepted* practice in most US restaurants.
This view is now widely *accepted* among scientists.

position: both — *an accepting community*; *her parents were very accepting*

senses.gloss: Willing to accept people or situations as they are, without judging.
examples: His family was *accepting* when he came out.
Young people tend to be *more accepting* of change.
It's a small but very *accepting* church.

position: both — *an accessible entrance*; *the park is accessible by bus*
takes: *to* + person: *accessible to everyone*; *by* + means: *accessible by car*
contrast: Russian *доступный* also means *cheap*; for price, English says *affordable*, not *accessible*.

senses.gloss: Easy to reach, enter or use, including for people with disabilities.
examples: The island is only *accessible* by boat.
All the restrooms are wheelchair *accessible*.
The new website is *more accessible* to people who are blind.

senses.gloss: Easy to understand or enjoy.
examples: The book explains quantum physics in an *accessible* way.
Her music is *more accessible* than her early albums.

position: both — *an accident-prone kid*; *I'm so accident-prone*

senses.gloss: Often having accidents, falling or breaking things.
examples: My son is so *accident-prone* that the ER nurses know his name.
She's the *most accident-prone* person I know.
Tired drivers are more *accident-prone*.

position: both — *an accidental discovery*; *the fire was accidental*

senses.gloss: Happening by chance or by mistake, not planned.
examples: Penicillin was an *accidental* discovery.
Investigators say the fire was *accidental*.
The report blamed the deaths on *accidental* overdoses.

position: both — *an accommodating host*; *the hotel staff were very accommodating*

senses.gloss: Willing to help and to change plans to fit what other people need.
examples: The restaurant was very *accommodating* about my food allergies.
My boss is *accommodating* when I need to leave early for my kids.
The second landlord was much *more accommodating* than the first.

position: attributive only — *the accompanying letter*; after a verb use the verb: *the letter that accompanies it*

senses.gloss: Going or coming together with something else.
examples: Please read the *accompanying* instructions before you start.
The article and the *accompanying* photos got a lot of attention.
A fever and *accompanying* headache are common side effects.

position: both — *an accomplished pianist*; *she is very accomplished*

senses.gloss: Very skilled at something, usually after years of practice.
examples: He's an *accomplished* chef and a published author.
Both of her daughters are *accomplished* musicians.
She was the *most accomplished* player on the team.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *they must be held accountable*; also *an accountable government*
takes: *for* + what you did or are in charge of: *accountable for the mistake*; *to* + the person or group you answer to: *accountable to voters*
contrast: The fixed phrase is *hold someone accountable*. *Responsible* is the everyday word; *accountable* stresses having to explain your actions and accept the consequences.

senses.gloss: Expected to explain your decisions and actions and to accept blame if something goes wrong.
examples: The officers involved should be held *accountable*.
Managers are *accountable* for their team's results.
Voters want a *more accountable* city council.

position: both — *an accredited university*; *the program is fully accredited*
takes: *by* + the official body: *accredited by the state*

senses.gloss: Officially approved as meeting the required standards.
examples: Make sure the college is *accredited* before you pay tuition.
Only *accredited* journalists were allowed into the briefing.
The hospital is *accredited* by a national commission.

position: attributive only — *accrued interest*; after a verb use the verb: *interest has accrued*

senses.gloss: Built up gradually over time, used about money, interest and time off.
examples: The loan balance includes *accrued* interest.
You'll be paid for any *accrued* vacation days when you leave.
The company reported its *accrued* expenses for the year.

position: attributive only — *accumulated wealth*; after a verb use the verb: *the snow had accumulated*

senses.gloss: Gathered or built up gradually over a period of time.
examples: It took a whole day to clear the *accumulated* snow.
The book draws on thirty years of *accumulated* experience.
They lost most of their *accumulated* savings in the crash.

position: both — *an accusatory tone*; *his questions sounded accusatory*

senses.gloss: Suggesting that someone has done something wrong.
examples: Try not to use an *accusatory* tone when you bring it up.
Her emails got *more accusatory* as the project fell behind.
The letter was polite but clearly *accusatory*.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *an accusing look*

senses.gloss: Showing that you think someone has done something wrong.
examples: She gave me an *accusing* look when the cake went missing.
Everyone pointed an *accusing* finger at the referee.
His voice wasn't angry, just quietly *accusing*.

position: attributive only — *an ace pilot*; after a verb say *excellent*
contrast: Mostly a noun (*an ace*, the playing card or an expert) and a verb (*I aced the test*). *That's ace!* as praise is British; in the US the adjective goes before a noun that names a skill: *an ace mechanic*.

senses.gloss: Extremely skilled at something.
examples: Her dad was an *ace* pilot in the Air Force.
The paper hired an *ace* reporter from Chicago.
We need an *ace* mechanic to figure out that noise.

position: both — *an acerbic critic*; *her reviews can be acerbic*

senses.gloss: Sharp and critical in a clever but unkind way, used about people, words and humor.
examples: The show is famous for its *acerbic* humor.
He wrote an *acerbic* review of the new restaurant.
Her comments got *more acerbic* as the night went on.

position: both — *an achievable goal*; *the target is achievable*

senses.gloss: Possible to do or reach with effort.
examples: Set small, *achievable* goals for each week.
Is a four-hour marathon *achievable* for a beginner?
Breaking the project into steps made it feel *more achievable*.

position: attributive only — *aching muscles*; in *my back is aching* the word is the verb

senses.gloss: Hurting with a dull, steady pain.
examples: A hot bath helps my *aching* back.
After the hike we collapsed on the couch with *aching* feet.

senses.gloss: Felt very strongly, as sadness or longing.
examples: The song is full of *aching* sadness.
She felt an *aching* loneliness after he left.

position: both — *achy joints*; *I feel achy all over*

senses.gloss: Having dull pains in the body, often when you are sick or tired.
senses.ru: ноющий, ломящий; с ломотой в теле
examples: I woke up tired and *achy*, so I think I'm getting the flu.
Cold weather makes my knees *achy*.
The day after the game I felt even *achier*.

position: both — *an acid taste*; *the soil is acid*
contrast: In *acid rain* and *acid reflux* the word is a noun used before another noun. For the chemistry sense Americans more often say *acidic*.

senses.gloss: Sharp and sour in taste.
examples: The wine was too *acid* for my taste.
Lemons have an *acid* flavor that cuts through rich food.

senses.gloss: Critical and unkind in a clever, biting way.
examples: The critic is known for her *acid* wit.
He made a few *acid* remarks about his former boss.

senses.gloss: Containing acid; having a pH below 7.
examples: Blueberries grow best in *acid* soil.
The water in the lake has become *more acid* over the years.

position: both — *acidic soil*; *tomatoes are acidic*

senses.gloss: Containing acid; having a pH below 7.
examples: Coffee and soda are both fairly *acidic*.
Oceans are becoming *more acidic* as they absorb carbon dioxide.

senses.gloss: Tasting sour and sharp.
examples: This orange juice is too *acidic* for my stomach.
Add a little sugar if the sauce tastes *acidic*.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *the acknowledged leader*; after a verb: *his talent is widely acknowledged*

senses.gloss: Generally accepted or recognized as being something.
examples: She is an *acknowledged* expert on climate policy.
He was the *acknowledged* leader of the group.
The risks of the plan are widely *acknowledged*.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *an acoustic guitar*; after a verb: *the show was acoustic*

senses.gloss: Played without electric amplification.
examples: He brought his *acoustic* guitar to the campfire.
The band played an *acoustic* set at the record store.
Tonight's concert is fully *acoustic*.

senses.gloss: Relating to sound or to how well sound carries in a place.
examples: The hall's *acoustic* design is the best in the city.
Engineers measured the *acoustic* properties of the new material.

position: predicative only — *we're acquainted*, *get acquainted*; never before a noun
takes: *with* + person or thing: *acquainted with the neighbors*, *acquainted with the rules*
contrast: Russian *знакомый* before a noun is not *acquainted*: *a familiar face*, *an acquaintance*. The common phrase is *get acquainted* or *get to know each other*.

senses.gloss: Knowing someone because you have met them, though not closely.
examples: Are you two *acquainted*?
We got *acquainted* at a friend's barbecue.

senses.gloss: Knowing about something because you have seen, read or used it.
examples: New employees should get *acquainted* with the safety rules.
After a week I was *more acquainted* with the neighborhood.

position: attributive only — *an acquired taste*; after a verb use the verb: *the habit was acquired*
contrast: *An acquired taste* is something most people dislike at first but can learn to like: *Blue cheese is an acquired taste*.

senses.gloss: Gained or developed during your life, not present from birth.
examples: Coffee is an *acquired* taste for most kids.
The condition is *acquired*, not inherited.
Reading music is an *acquired* skill.

position: both — *an acquisitive society*; *the company has become acquisitive*

senses.gloss: Eager to get more money, possessions or, for a company, other businesses.
examples: Critics say we live in an *acquisitive* culture.
The tech giant has been especially *acquisitive* this year.
He grew *more acquisitive* as his fortune grew.

position: both — *acrid smoke*; *the air was acrid*

senses.gloss: Sharp and unpleasant to smell or taste, often burning the nose or throat.
examples: *Acrid* smoke filled the kitchen.
The air near the plant was *acrid* and hard to breathe.
The smell got *more acrid* as we got closer to the fire.

position: both — *an acrimonious divorce*; *the debate became acrimonious*

senses.gloss: Full of anger and bitter arguments.
examples: They went through an *acrimonious* divorce.
The town hall meeting quickly turned *acrimonious*.
It was one of the *most acrimonious* campaigns in years.

position: both — *an acrobatic catch*; *the dancers were incredibly acrobatic*

senses.gloss: Involving or showing difficult, athletic movements like jumping, flipping and balancing.
examples: The receiver made an *acrobatic* catch in the end zone.
The circus show was full of *acrobatic* stunts.
Her routine this year is even *more acrobatic*.

position: attributive only — hyphenated before a noun: *across-the-board cuts*; after a verb *across the board* is an adverb phrase, without hyphens
form: compound — preposition phrase *across the board*, hyphenated before a noun
contrast: *Prices rose across the board* uses the adverb phrase; only *an across-the-board increase* is the adjective.

senses.gloss: Affecting everyone or everything in a group equally.
examples: The city announced *across-the-board* budget cuts.
Workers got an *across-the-board* raise of three percent.
The new rules call for *across-the-board* testing in every school.

position: attributive only — *the acting director*
form: -ing from *act* (to do a job for someone)
contrast: Russian *действующий* before a job title is usually *current*, not *acting*: *the current president*. *Acting* means temporary, until someone is officially appointed. The noun *acting* is the profession.

senses.gloss: Doing someone else's job for a short time, until a permanent person is chosen.
examples: She was named *acting* principal after Mr. Lee retired.
The *acting* police chief spoke to reporters.
He served as *acting* CEO for six months.

ru: практически применимый; дающий основание для иска
position: both — *actionable advice*; *the statement may be actionable*

senses.gloss: Clear and practical enough to act on right away.
examples: The report gives managers *actionable* recommendations.
We need feedback that is *more actionable* than 'do better'.

senses.gloss: In law, giving someone a reason to sue.
examples: His lawyer said the false claims were *actionable*.
Not every rude comment is legally *actionable*.

position: both — *activated charcoal*; *your new card is activated*

senses.gloss: Made ready to work, or switched on.
examples: Once your account is *activated*, you can log in.
Make sure the alarm is *activated* before you leave.
The phone stays locked until it is *activated*.

senses.gloss: Treated with heat or chemicals so that it works better, as charcoal.
examples: The water filter contains *activated* carbon.
Doctors sometimes give *activated* charcoal after a poisoning.

position: both — *an active lifestyle*; *she's very active*
takes: *in* + noun or *-ing* — taking part: *active in local politics*
contrast: Russian *активный* is often *active*, but *активный отдых* is an *active vacation* or *outdoor activities*, and *активные продажи* is *proactive sales*.

senses.gloss: Moving around and doing physical things; full of energy.
examples: My grandmother is still very *active* at eighty.
Kids need to stay *active* during the summer.
I've been *more active* since I got a dog.

senses.gloss: Taking part in something and working hard at it.
examples: He's an *active* member of the PTA.
She has always been *active* in her church.

senses.gloss: Working, operating or happening now.
examples: Mount St. Helens is still an *active* volcano.
Your account is no longer *active*.
Police are treating it as an *active* investigation.

senses.gloss: In grammar, having a subject that does the action of the verb.
examples: "The dog bit the man" is in the *active* voice.
Editors usually prefer *active* verbs.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *an activist judge*; after a verb: *the court has become more activist*
contrast: Usually a noun (*a climate activist*). The adjective is common in US politics and business: *an activist judge* makes new policy through rulings; *activist investors* push a company to change.

senses.gloss: Working hard and openly to bring about political, social or business change.
examples: Critics call her an *activist* judge.
An *activist* investor bought a large stake in the company.
The Supreme Court became *more activist* in the 1960s.

position: attributive only — *actuarial tables*
contrast: Nothing to do with Russian *актуальный* (current, relevant). That is *relevant*, *topical* or *up-to-date*.

senses.gloss: Relating to calculating risks and costs for insurance and pensions.
examples: Insurers use *actuarial* tables to set life insurance prices.
She passed her first *actuarial* exam in college.
The pension fund hired an *actuarial* firm to review its numbers.

position: both — *an acute shortage*; *the problem is acute*

senses.gloss: Very serious or severe.
examples: There is an *acute* shortage of nurses in rural hospitals.
The housing crisis is *most acute* in big cities.
She felt *acute* embarrassment when her phone rang during the funeral.

senses.gloss: In medicine, starting suddenly and quickly becoming severe.
examples: He was rushed to the hospital with *acute* appendicitis.
The clinic treats *acute* injuries, not long-term conditions.

senses.gloss: Very sensitive or sharp, used about the senses and the mind.
examples: Dogs have an *acute* sense of smell.
She's an *acute* observer of small-town life.

senses.gloss: In geometry, less than 90 degrees.
examples: Draw an *acute* angle and label it.
Every triangle has at least two *acute* angles.

ru: специальный, созданный для конкретной цели; импровизированный
position: both — *an ad hoc committee*; *the process was pretty ad hoc*
contrast: In *decisions were made ad hoc* it is an adverb. The adjective can sound negative: 'unplanned, not systematic'.

senses.gloss: Made or done for one particular purpose or situation, often without planning.
examples: The board formed an *ad hoc* committee to study the problem.
Our hiring process is too *ad hoc*; we need clear rules.
The repairs were done on an *ad hoc* basis.

position: attributive only — *an ad hominem attack*

senses.gloss: Attacking the person who makes an argument instead of the argument itself.
senses.ru: переходящий на личности, направленный против человека, а не его доводов
examples: Calling her stupid is an *ad hominem* attack, not a counterargument.
The debate turned into a series of *ad hominem* insults.
Please avoid *ad hominem* comments in this forum.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *she was adamant*; also *an adamant refusal*
takes: *about* + noun or *-ing*: *adamant about staying*; *that*-clause: *adamant that he was innocent*
contrast: Stress the first syllable: AD-uh-muhnt. It describes a person's position, not a hard material, in modern English.

senses.gloss: Refusing to change your opinion or decision.
examples: He was *adamant* that he had locked the door.
My parents were *adamant* about finishing college first.
She became even *more adamant* after reading the report.

position: both — *an adaptable employee*; *kids are very adaptable*

senses.gloss: Able to change or be changed easily to fit new situations.
examples: Raccoons are *adaptable* animals that do well in cities.
We need someone *adaptable* who can handle last-minute changes.
Younger workers are often *more adaptable* to new technology.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *adaptive equipment*; after a verb: *the system is adaptive*
contrast: *Adaptable* describes a person or thing that can change; *adaptive* is more technical — designed to adjust, or helping someone adjust: *adaptive cruise control*, *adaptive sports*.

senses.gloss: Designed to change and adjust to different conditions or needs.
examples: The new car has *adaptive* cruise control.
The software uses *adaptive* learning to match each student's level.

senses.gloss: Made for people with disabilities so they can take part in an activity.
examples: The resort offers *adaptive* skiing lessons.
Her school provides *adaptive* equipment for students who need it.

position: both — *an addictive drug*; *this game is addictive*
contrast: *Addictive* is the thing that causes the habit; *addicted* is the person who has it: *The app is addictive, and I'm addicted to it*.

senses.gloss: Causing a strong need to keep using or doing it.
examples: Nicotine is highly *addictive*.
These chips are dangerously *addictive*.
Some experts say social media is *more addictive* than TV.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *additional costs*; after a verb: *shipping is additional*

senses.gloss: Added to what already exists; extra.
examples: There's an *additional* fee for checked bags.
For *additional* information, visit our website.
Delivery is available, but the cost is *additional*.

position: both — *an addled mind*; *my brain is totally addled*

senses.gloss: Confused and unable to think clearly.
examples: After two nights without sleep, my brain was completely *addled*.
He gave a rambling, *addled* speech.
The medicine left her *more addled* than before.

position: both — *an adept negotiator*; *she's adept at handling clients*
takes: *at* + noun or *-ing*: *adept at fixing things*; *in* + noun: *adept in several languages*
contrast: The adjective is stressed uh-DEPT. The noun *adept* (an expert) is often AD-ept, and Russian *адепт* (a follower) is closer to *follower* or *devotee*.

senses.gloss: Very good at doing something that takes skill.
examples: He's *adept* at getting kids to eat vegetables.
She is an *adept* politician.
Teenagers are often *more adept* with technology than their parents.

position: both — *adequate funding*; *the space is adequate*
takes: *for* + noun: *adequate for our needs*; *to*-infinitive: *adequate to cover the costs*
contrast: False friend: Russian *адекватный* about a person (sane, reasonable) is *reasonable*, *sensible* or *normal*. English *adequate* means 'enough' or 'just OK'. Stress: AD-i-kwuht, not ad-e-KWAYT.

senses.gloss: Enough in amount or good enough for a particular need.
examples: Make sure you get *adequate* sleep before the exam.
The apartment is small but *adequate* for two people.
Many schools still lack *adequate* funding.

senses.gloss: Acceptable but not especially good.
examples: The food was *adequate*, but nothing special.
His performance was *adequate* at best.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *adhesive tape*; after a verb: *the back of the label is adhesive*
contrast: Also a noun: *a strong adhesive* (a glue).

senses.gloss: Able to stick to a surface; sticky.
examples: Put an *adhesive* bandage on the cut.
The hooks have an *adhesive* back, so you don't need nails.
Peel off the paper to expose the *adhesive* side.

position: both — *an adjacent room*; *the parking lot is adjacent to the school*

senses.gloss: Next to or very near something else.
examples: The hotel is *adjacent* to the convention center.
We booked *adjacent* rooms so the kids could be near us.
Firefighters kept the fire from spreading to *adjacent* buildings.

position: attributive only — *an adjunct professor*
contrast: In US universities an *adjunct professor* is a part-time, non-permanent teacher, not a senior rank. Russian *адъюнкт* is a different, military-academic title.

senses.gloss: Working at a college on a part-time or temporary contract, not as permanent staff.
examples: He works as an *adjunct* professor at two community colleges.
Many *adjunct* instructors don't get health insurance.

senses.gloss: Added to something more important, as a support.
examples: The drug is used as an *adjunct* therapy alongside surgery.
The online course is an *adjunct* program to the main degree.

position: both — *an adjustable chair*; *the straps are adjustable*

senses.gloss: Possible to change in size, height or position.
examples: I bought an *adjustable* desk so I can stand while I work.
The seat height is fully *adjustable*.
The straps on this backpack are *adjustable*.

position: both — *adjusted figures*; *prices adjusted for inflation*; *he seems well adjusted*
takes: *for* + noun — corrected to allow for something: *adjusted for inflation*; *to* + noun — used to something new: *adjusted to the time change*

senses.gloss: Changed slightly to allow for a particular factor, used about numbers.
examples: *Adjusted* for inflation, wages have barely grown.
The *adjusted* numbers show a smaller loss.

senses.gloss: Used to a new situation and comfortable in it; emotionally stable.
examples: After a month, the kids were fully *adjusted* to the new school.
She's one of the *best-adjusted* people I know.

position: both — mostly before a noun: *administrative staff*; after a verb: *the delay was purely administrative*
contrast: *Administrative leave* in the US is time off, often paid, while an employee is investigated. Russian *административный штраф* is usually just *a fine*.

senses.gloss: Relating to managing and organizing the work of a business or organization.
examples: She works as an *administrative* assistant at a law firm.
Too much of a teacher's time goes to *administrative* tasks.
The officer was placed on *administrative* leave.

position: both — *an admirable goal*; *his honesty is admirable*
contrast: The stress moves: *adMIRE*, but *ADmirable*.

senses.gloss: Deserving respect and approval.
examples: She did an *admirable* job under difficult conditions.
His loyalty to his friends is *admirable*.
What makes her story *more admirable* is that she never complained.

position: both — *admissible evidence*; *the recording is not admissible*

senses.gloss: Allowed to be used or considered, especially as evidence in a court of law.
examples: The judge ruled that the confession was not *admissible*.
Lie detector results are rarely *admissible* in court.
The lawyers argued over which documents were *admissible* evidence.

position: both — *adolescent boys*; *his humor is a little adolescent*
contrast: Also a noun: *an adolescent*. In everyday speech Americans say *teenage* or *teen* for the first sense.

senses.gloss: Relating to young people between childhood and adulthood.
examples: The clinic specializes in *adolescent* mental health.
*Adolescent* girls are especially at risk.

senses.gloss: Behaving in a silly or immature way for an adult.
examples: The senator's *adolescent* jokes embarrassed his staff.
Their feud is getting *more adolescent* every week.

ru: которого можно взять из приюта, усыновить
position: both — *adoptable pets*; *all these puppies are adoptable*

senses.gloss: Ready and available to be adopted, especially a pet from a shelter.
senses.ru: доступный для усыновления, для взятия из приюта
examples: The shelter posts photos of *adoptable* dogs every week.
All of the cats in this room are *adoptable*.
Older children are just as *adoptable* as babies.

position: both — *an adopted daughter*; *I was adopted*
contrast: *Adopted* is the child: *their adopted son*. *Adoptive* is the parents or family: *his adoptive parents*.

senses.gloss: Legally taken into a family and raised as its own child.
examples: They have two biological kids and one *adopted* daughter.
She didn't find out she was *adopted* until she was twenty.

senses.gloss: Chosen as your own, though not where you were born.
examples: Chicago is his *adopted* hometown.
She speaks proudly of her *adopted* country.

position: attributive only — *adoptive parents*
contrast: *Adoptive* is the family who adopts; *adopted* is the child. ✗ *his adopted parents* → *his adoptive parents*.

senses.gloss: Having legally taken a child into the family as their own.
examples: His *adoptive* parents were at the wedding.
She has a close relationship with her *adoptive* family.
*Adoptive* mothers can get paid leave at many companies.
